title: Yellowstone National Park
prompt: Plan me a first-time-friendly 3-day Yellowstone trip with wildlife, geyser basins, scenic stops, and no crazy hikes. Keep the pacing realistic.
response:
I created a three-day Yellowstone plan that prioritizes the classics without turning each day into a marathon:

- **Day 1: Geyser country** — Old Faithful, an easy Upper Geyser Basin wander, and Grand Prismatic Spring.
- **Day 2: Canyon scenery and wildlife** — short canyon viewpoints followed by unhurried watching in Hayden Valley.
- **Day 3: Lamar Valley wildlife** — an early wildlife outing, with the afternoon kept light rather than adding another cross-park circuit.

I recommend **Canyon Village as the overnight base** for this version: it keeps the second day especially easy and makes Lamar more practical than staying outside the west entrance. Day 1 still involves substantial road time, so I left out extra basins and Mammoth rather than crowding them in.

This assumes **three full sightseeing days, a vehicle, and dates when the connecting roads are open**—not arrival and departure squeezed into those days. Walking is short and adjustable, with no strenuous hikes or steep canyon descents. Check [NPS road conditions](https://www.nps.gov/yell/planyourvisit/parkroads.htm) for your dates; this is not a winter-access itinerary.

What month are you going, and do you already have lodging? Those are the two details most likely to change the routing.
description: Three full days of geyser basins, canyon views and wildlife watching, with a Canyon Village base and short, adjustable walks.

plan.intro: Three full sightseeing days combining signature geysers, canyon views, and two contrasting wildlife valleys, with short adjustable walks rather than strenuous hikes. Recommended base: Canyon Village, including the night before Day 1. This plan assumes a vehicle and dates when connecting park roads are open; it is not a winter-access itinerary. Confirm road conditions and lodging operations for your dates. Road travel, parking, and wildlife delays need generous buffers; arrival and departure travel are outside these three days.

narrativeSections.heading: Practical essentials
narrativeSections.markdown: Stay at least **100 yards from bears and wolves** and **25 yards from bison and elk**; never approach wildlife or stop in the traffic lane. Bring binoculars, layers, water, and picnic supplies. Thermal areas require staying on designated boardwalks and trails. Yellowstone has no park-wide public transit, so this routing needs a vehicle or a separately arranged tour. Check [official road conditions](https://www.nps.gov/yell/planyourvisit/parkroads.htm) before travel; if a connecting road or basin is unavailable, adjust the affected day rather than forcing a long detour.

title: Glacier National Park
prompt: Plan me 5 days in Glacier in mid-July with realistic pacing, scenic drives, classic viewpoints, photography, and moderate or shorter hikes.
response:
I’ve built a five-day Glacier plan that moves west to east, with one main outing each day and room for photography rather than a packed checklist.

- **Day 1:** Cedar forest and Avalanche Lake, followed by a quiet afternoon.
- **Day 2:** Going-to-the-Sun Road and alpine scenery, moving to your east-side base.
- **Day 3:** A shorter waterfall hike and classic St. Mary Lake photography.
- **Day 4:** Many Glacier’s mountain-and-lake scenery, with your longest hike.
- **Day 5:** A gentler finish at Two Medicine.

I’ve assumed **five full sightseeing days**, a car for getting between areas, and lodging split between **West Glacier for the first night and St. Mary for the remaining nights**. Arrive on the west side the evening before Day 1 if possible. This avoids repeatedly crossing the park; returning to a west-side airport afterward needs additional travel time.

The main hiking tradeoff is **Grinnell Lake: roughly 7 miles round trip**, relatively gentle but longer than the other hikes. You can turn around earlier without committing to the full distance. This is not the much harder Grinnell Glacier hike.

**Mid-July can still mean snow at Logan Pass.** The saved plan includes a lower-elevation fallback for Hidden Lake Overlook. Road access, vehicle reservations, and shuttle arrangements must be checked for your travel year through [Glacier’s official planning pages](https://www.nps.gov/glac/planyourvisit/index.htm); I haven’t assumed a particular year’s rules apply.

If your five days include flights or you already have lodging, tell me—that would change the pacing and base arrangement.
description: Five full days from West Glacier to St. Mary, pairing classic hikes and lake photography with recovery time and a gentler Two Medicine finish.

images.alt: Jagged peaks rise out of a forested valley and an empty road curves off into the distance.

plan.intro: Five full sightseeing days in mid-July, sequenced west to east with one principal outing per day. Assumes arrival near West Glacier the evening before Day 1 and a car for travel between areas; no flight or departure-day logistics are included. Stay near West Glacier for Night 1 and St. Mary for Nights 2–5. The final night is optional if continuing elsewhere. Allow extra travel time after this itinerary for a west-side departure. Hiking distances below are approximate; durations include photo breaks rather than just moving time.

narrativeSections.heading: Before your July visit
narrativeSections.markdown:
**Access and reservations:** Confirm Going-to-the-Sun Road opening, any vehicle-reservation requirements, Many Glacier access, and the shuttle arrangements for your travel year on [Glacier's official planning pages](https://www.nps.gov/glac/planyourvisit/index.htm). Do not assume an entrance pass covers a separate reservation or that a shuttle works as a cross-park luggage transfer. This itinerary's road crossing depends on permitted access; a car does not guarantee parking.

**Snow and weather:** Mid-July can still have snow on alpine trails. Check ranger advice and trail conditions before the Hidden Lake outing; do not cross steep snow without appropriate skills and equipment. Lower-elevation lake time is the fallback. Carry rain layers and sun protection, and adjust exposed outings for thunderstorms.

**Wildlife and photography:** Carry readily accessible bear spray and know how to use it; keep official wildlife distances and never approach animals for a photograph. Pack water and picnic lunches. Early starts help with parking and photography, but this plan does not require dawn starts every day.

title: Utah Mighty 5
prompt: Plan a realistic 7-day Utah Mighty 5 road trip covering Zion, Bryce Canyon, Capitol Reef, Arches, and Canyonlands. Keep the driving realistic and don’t cram every day.
response:
I’ve built a **west-to-east, 7-day road trip** that covers all five parks without trying to add a major hike every day:

- **Day 1:** Las Vegas to Springdale, with a gentle afternoon.
- **Day 2:** A full Zion day.
- **Day 3:** Move to Bryce Canyon for hoodoo scenery.
- **Day 4:** Take scenic UT-12 to Torrey, with a light Capitol Reef introduction.
- **Day 5:** More Capitol Reef, then move to Moab.
- **Day 6:** Arches, with an afternoon break.
- **Day 7:** Canyonlands’ Island in the Sky district, then a final night in Moab.

The key is **two nights in Springdale, one near Bryce, one in Torrey, and three in Moab**. Capitol Reef gets time across two days rather than becoming a roadside checkbox, and you won’t change hotels between Arches and Canyonlands.

**Assumptions:** Start in Las Vegas on Day 1 and leave from Salt Lake City **the day after Day 7**. This is seven road-trip days—not seven days including both flights. Returning to Las Vegas would add substantial backtracking. If flights must fit inside the seven days, tell me; that needs a tighter version.

The saved plan includes generous transfer allowances rather than treating nonstop driving times as the whole travel day. Walks are optional and mostly short; the Arches plan uses the distant Delicate Arch viewpoint, **not** the strenuous hike to the arch itself.

Spring or fall generally makes this easier than summer heat or winter snow. Once you choose dates, check Zion’s shuttle arrangements, Arches entry requirements, and road/trail conditions before committing to the daily details.

Transfer blocks are generous planning allowances, not confirmed route durations.

narrativeSections.markdown:
This undated itinerary assumes suitable road and walking conditions, not confirmed openings. Check Zion transportation arrangements, Arches timed-entry requirements for your dates, and each park’s road/trail alerts. Bryce’s seasonal shuttle is generally recommended rather than mandatory for ordinary passenger cars ([NPS shuttle guidance](https://www.nps.gov/brca/planyourvisit/shuttle.htm)); large vehicles have additional restrictions. If an outing is unavailable, substitute accessible roadside scenery rather than a more demanding hike. Avoid exposed walks in dangerous heat or storms; snow and ice can affect Bryce and higher roads.

Allow a separate travel day after Day 7 for Moab to Salt Lake City and a conservative airport buffer—preferably an overnight before an early flight. A Las Vegas round trip requires materially more driving. UT-12 is a scenic mountain route, not a shortcut to rush. Transfer allowances here are planning buffers; actual routes and timing depend on dates and conditions.

title: Alaska National Parks
prompt: Plan a paced 10-day Alaska national parks trip that hits the major highlights without feeling rushed. Be realistic about travel time and logistics.
response:
I’ve built a paced 10-day trip around **Denali and Kenai Fjords**, with Anchorage as the gateway. Two parks is the right balance here: you get Alaska’s mountain-and-wildlife interior and its glacier-and-ocean coast without spending the trip chasing flights.

- **Day 1:** Arrive and recover in Anchorage.
- **Day 2:** Travel north and settle into the Denali area.
- **Day 3:** Denali’s signature park-bus experience.
- **Day 4:** A flexible Denali walking and scenery day.
- **Day 5:** Return to Anchorage, breaking up the long journey south.
- **Day 6:** Scenic travel to Seward, with an unhurried afternoon.
- **Day 7:** Kenai Fjords glacier-and-wildlife cruise.
- **Day 8:** Exit Glacier and a relaxed afternoon; also useful cruise-weather flexibility.
- **Day 9:** Return to Anchorage, protecting your flight home from a same-day highway transfer.
- **Day 10:** Depart.

**Assumptions:** these are 10 days including arrival and departure, in summer—ideally June through August—with a rental car recommended for the land portions. You’ll have three nights near Denali and three in Seward. For planning, leave roughly **6–7 hours including breaks** for each Anchorage–Denali travel day and **3–4 hours including stops** between Anchorage and Seward; these are generous planning allowances, not confirmed route times.

Choose a Seward cruise that explicitly includes **Kenai Fjords National Park and a tidewater glacier**, rather than only a shorter Resurrection Bay outing. Allow most of the day, and keep the following day movable if the operator can accommodate a weather change—there’s no guarantee of rescheduling.

Denali bus access varies by season and road conditions. The [NPS currently describes a Mile 43 turnaround](https://www.nps.gov/dena/planyourvisit/shuttles.htm); confirm the route for your travel dates rather than expecting access to the entire park road. Neither mountain views nor wildlife sightings are guaranteed.

I’ve left out Katmai, Lake Clark and the more remote parks deliberately: adding one would mean extra flight logistics, cost and weather exposure, or taking away the breathing room you asked for. If you share your month and preferred walking difficulty, we can refine this framework without cramming in more destinations.

title: Yosemite National Park
prompt: Plan a clean 3-day first-time Yosemite itinerary with Valley views, one moderate hike, scenic stops, and enough downtime that the weekend doesn’t feel rushed.
response:
I created a relaxed three-day Yosemite plan with one main focus each day:

- **Day 1:** Classic Valley views and easy meadow-and-waterfall walks.
- **Day 2:** A moderate hike to Vernal Fall Footbridge, followed by an intentionally free afternoon.
- **Day 3:** Glacier Point’s big panorama and a final Valley scenic stop, without adding another demanding hike.

The sequence gives you Yosemite’s signature scenery without turning every day into a checklist. I assumed **three full sightseeing days**, a base in Yosemite Valley, and access to a car for the scenic overlooks; arrival and departure travel are additional. El Portal is an alternative base, but adds commuting.

Glacier Point is seasonal, and current road and trail conditions haven’t been confirmed for your dates. The plan includes a Valley-based fallback; check [Yosemite’s official guidance](https://www.nps.gov/yose/index.htm) for access and any entry-reservation requirements before traveling. Share your month and whether these three days include travel, and I can refine the fit.

images.alt: Granite dome with trace amounts of snow.

plan.intro: Three full sightseeing days: classic Valley scenery, one moderate hike with recovery time, then high-country views without another strenuous outing. Assumes a car is available for the overlooks, not that transportation is booked.

Check [Yosemite's official website](https://www.nps.gov/yose/index.htm) for road and trail conditions, any entry-reservation requirements, and date-specific transportation details. Use the [Valley shuttle](https://www.nps.gov/yose/planyourvisit/publictransportation.htm) where practical rather than repeatedly moving the car.

Glacier Point Road is seasonal. If it is unavailable, replace that excursion with a leisurely Valley morning and an optional short Mirror Lake walk, retaining the afternoon rest and Valley View stop. Snow or ice can also make the footbridge hike unsuitable: confirm conditions before setting out; if unsafe, substitute an easier Valley walk rather than forcing the moderate hike. Carry water, snacks, layers and footwear with traction.

title: Grand Canyon + Page
prompt: Plan a 4-day Grand Canyon trip that also includes Page, with one major scenic day, viewpoints, and one deliberately relaxed day.
response:
I’ve built a four-day route from the Grand Canyon’s South Rim to Page, with the biggest scenery day followed by a genuine day off.

- **Day 1:** Settle into the canyon landscape with rim views and unhurried exploring.
- **Day 2:** Your major scenic day—Desert View, the move to Page, and Horseshoe Bend.
- **Day 3:** Deliberately relaxed in Page: sleep in, linger over meals, and leave the afternoon free.
- **Day 4:** A lighter Page finale with a canyon overlook and flexible Lake Powell exploration.

The plan uses **one night near the South Rim and two nights in Page**, avoiding a return drive to the canyon. Day 2 carries the most travel and walking; Day 3 has no required sightseeing or long drive.

I assumed four usable days, a car for travel between areas, and no long airport transfers within those days. Dates will determine daylight, heat, road conditions, and local access arrangements. Tell me your travel month and starting/ending city if you’d like those logistics fitted in.

title: Olympic National Park
prompt: Plan a 4-day Olympic National Park road trip with mountains, rainforest, and coast, but keep the driving realistic.
response:
I’ve planned a north-to-south route that keeps mountains, rainforest and coast on separate, unrushed days:

- **Day 1:** Hurricane Ridge mountain scenery.
- **Day 2:** Lake Crescent, then move west to Forks.
- **Day 3:** A dedicated Hoh Rain Forest day.
- **Day 4:** Ruby Beach and a finish near Lake Quinault.

Stay in **Port Angeles after Day 1 and Forks for the next two nights**. Changing bases once mid-trip avoids repeatedly crossing the peninsula. Budget roughly **2–3 hours on the road most days**, as a planning allowance rather than confirmed driving times; entrance queues and stops are extra.

I assumed four full sightseeing days, starting in Port Angeles and ending near Quinault, with travel to and from the peninsula outside those days. Returning to Seattle on Day 4 would mean cutting back the coastal day.

Your month matters most for Hurricane Ridge access. Summer into early fall generally makes this combination simplest; check road access and any entry or shuttle requirements for your dates. If traveling imminently, [NPS reports](https://www.nps.gov/olym/index.htm) overnight US 101 closures at Hoh River Bridge October 13–19, 2026, which could affect this route.

What month are you going, and does Day 4 need to end in Seattle?

title: Big Bend National Park
prompt: Plan a weekend in Big Bend focused on dark skies, Milky Way photography, scenic windows, and easy photo-friendly timing.
response:
I created a photography-first Big Bend weekend with short walks and room to recover between good-light windows.

- **Saturday:** easy preparation, mountain framing at the Window, and a flexible dark-sky session.
- **Sunday:** sleep recovery, broad desert views at Sotol Vista, then departure.

I assumed Friday arrival, two nights near Study Butte/Terlingua, and a car available locally. This keeps the weekend focused rather than adding long hikes or compulsory sunrise starts.

**Choose the moon window before choosing the weekend.** Aim for moonless shooting near new moon. The Milky Way’s bright core is generally visible roughly March–October: spring often favors pre-dawn sessions, while late summer and early fall offer easier evening opportunities. Winter offers beautiful stars, but not the bright core.

The Window View Trail is the easy 0.3-mile paved loop, not the longer Window Trail. Chisos Basin and nighttime access still need confirmation for your dates; check [NPS alerts](https://www.nps.gov/bibe/index.htm). The plan includes a lower-elevation fallback if the Basin is unavailable.

Bring a tripod, spare batteries and a dim red headlamp, and scout your night foreground in daylight. What month or weekend are you considering? That determines the moon window and whether the photography session fits after sunset or before dawn.

No dates are assigned. Milky Way timing depends on season and moonrise/moonset: target a moonless window, generally March–October for the bright core. If the Basin is inaccessible, substitute a relaxed lower-elevation landscape session at an accessible designated overlook. title: Washington’s National Parks
prompt: Plan a realistic 7-day Washington national parks trip covering Olympic, Mount Rainier, and North Cascades without turning it into a driving marathon.
response:
I built a seven-day Seattle loop with **two dedicated travel days**, rather than squeezing sightseeing into every long drive.

- **Day 1:** Olympic’s Lake Crescent, then settle into Forks.
- **Day 2:** Rain forest and Pacific coast, with a second night in Forks.
- **Day 3:** Move to the Mount Rainier area; keep the rest of the day easy.
- **Day 4:** A full Paradise day for mountain scenery and walking.
- **Day 5:** Move north to Marblemount, without another mountain detour.
- **Day 6:** North Cascades lake-and-mountain scenery, with unhurried exploration.
- **Day 7:** Return to Seattle with a generous buffer.

**The compromise:** seven days covering all three parks still involves substantial driving. This version protects four sightseeing days and avoids repeated long commutes by staying two nights each in Forks, Ashford and Marblemount. I left out Hurricane Ridge, Sunrise and an east-side Cascades extension—not because they aren’t worthwhile, but because they would undermine your main goal.

I assumed **Seattle start/end, a car, and seven usable days**, ideally late July through September. Arrive before Day 1; avoid an early flight on Day 7. Dates, hiking ability and current access still need confirming; the saved plan includes the relevant checks. If you want demanding hikes rather than shorter walks, that’s the main refinement I’d make.

narrativeSections.markdown: This summer-style itinerary depends on mountain roads and trails being suitable for your dates. Confirm road access, any required shuttle arrangements, entry reservations and trail conditions with [Olympic](https://www.nps.gov/olym/planyourvisit/index.htm), [Mount Rainier](https://www.nps.gov/mora/planyourvisit/basicinfo.htm) and [North Cascades](https://www.nps.gov/noca/planyourvisit/index.htm). No date-specific access or reservation requirement has been confirmed here. If high-elevation conditions prevent Paradise walking, use suitable lower-elevation outings instead; outside the summer access season the overall route may need redesigning. Check coastal weather and tides before beach walking. This North Cascades visit focuses on the accessible park complex rather than a strenuous hike into the national park interior.

title: Acadia National Park
prompt: Plan a fall weekend in Acadia with sunrise, scenic drives, easy-to-moderate walks, and the best autumn atmosphere.
response:
I planned two full sightseeing days, using Bar Harbor as the suggested base:

- **Day 1:** Cadillac sunrise, coastal scenery and a leisurely Park Loop Road outing.
- **Day 2:** Woodland color, Jordan Pond and a cozy autumn finish in town.

This balances Acadia’s dramatic coast with its quieter fall atmosphere, without strenuous summit hikes. Aim for **early to mid-October** for a good chance of colorful foliage; peak timing varies each year.

I assumed you arrive the evening before and have a car available locally. Cadillac’s sunrise drive depends on road access and the applicable vehicle reservation; confirm those for your dates. The saved plan includes a coastal sunrise fallback. There is also a current repair closure on southern Ocean Path, so check [park alerts](https://www.nps.gov/acad/index.htm) before walking it.

Share your dates and whether Sunday includes travel home, and I can tailor the weekend’s timing.
description: A fall weekend combining sunrise, coastal scenery and woodland walks, with a Bar Harbor base and time to slow down.

images.alt: A man and woman holding walking sticks hike up a mountain summit near a wooden trail sign.
images.credit: Photo courtesy of Sam Mallon, Friends of Acadia

plan.intro: A two-day fall sightseeing weekend pairing sunrise and ocean scenery with woodland color and pond views. Assumes arrival the preceding evening, two full sightseeing days and a car available locally; Bar Harbor is the recommended overnight base. Early to mid-October is a good general target for foliage, not a guarantee of peak color. Follow signed road directions on Park Loop Road and allow extra time for parking and unhurried stops.

narrativeSections.heading: Before you go
narrativeSections.markdown: Confirm road access, trail conditions and seasonal services for your actual dates. Cadillac’s sunrise drive requires the applicable vehicle reservation during its reservation season; check the date-specific requirements on the [official Cadillac driving page](https://www.nps.gov/thingstodo/drive-cadillac-mountain.htm). If sunrise access is unavailable, substitute a coastal dawn outing on an accessible section of Ocean Path rather than attempting a difficult predawn hike. Check [Acadia alerts](https://www.nps.gov/acad/index.htm) for Ocean Path repair limits and other changes. Bring an appropriate park entrance pass. Do not rely on the seasonal Island Explorer without confirming its dates and schedule. Pack layers, rain protection, grippy shoes and picnic supplies; shorter fall daylight rewards keeping the afternoons flexible.

stops.note: Choose a short out-and-back on an open section, turning around after roughly 30–45 minutes. Stay on the path rather than wet shoreline rocks. Confirm repair limits for your dates; if restricted, shorten the walk rather than bypass barriers.

stops.note: Enjoy the pond views and choose a short shoreline out-and-back, about 60–90 minutes at your pace. The full circuit has uneven footing and is not necessary for this weekend’s easier walking focus.
